title: 13th Special Service: music department and the soldiers' chorale
summary: Trained in chemical warfare, he drifted into music, helped found the 13th Special Service as head of music, and led a 12-voice chorale that toured the front and played Paris's Madeleine Theatre.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well, when you went over what was your company doing?
Well, I was in the smoke company, they called it. You know, camouflage.
I was trained in chemical warfare.
Yeah. So you didn't get into special services?
Yeah. Yeah, I got in after the -- you know, I went there as a smoke -- a chemical -- engineer.
Yeah. Part of the company that -- yeah.

But little by little I began to form little groups and they began to sing and then played in the church, and finally they made a company, the 13th Special Service, and I was head of the music department. And they elected a colored Lieutenant, Lieutenant Chaney (PHONETIC). So they put him over the company. So we formed the 13th Special Service right there.
And I used to teach all -- I had 12 voices.
Kids who, you know, we picked out.
Kids who had at least a little talent.
We wouldn't pick out, you know, anyone.
But the kids who really had voices, and I'd listen to them and think yeah, I want you, I want you. And we formed a chorale of 12 voices, and we toured, all up to the front lines and everywhere.

Well, things like, 'Deep Purple,' 'Sleepy Lagoon,' a song that just came out -- what was that song. We used to play it at the Officers' Club and one of the Colonel's wives used to ask for it all the time. 'Sentimental Journey.'

And I would teach them every note, and they would remember, and I would wake them up in the morning and say, 'Now, let's go over it without the piano.' And they would -- I'd say, 'Do you remember your note?' He'd say, 'Yeah, Kenny, I've got it.' Because they knew they had to do it or either go over, you know.

So we -- I mean it was so wonderful, when we came to Paris we played at the Madeleine Theater, and there was a General Biddle who was chief of the Parisian area, who really hung down from the balcony and said, 'Great. Great, Sergeant. Wonderful work.' And Gertrude Stein and Alice B. Toklas were there, and they would say, 'How do you find time to do all this?' You know.
